problems.title: Two Sum
problems.problem: Given an array of integers `nums` and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two numbers such that they add up to `target`. Exactly one valid answer exists, and you may not use the same element twice.
examples: twoSum([0, 4, 3, 0], 0)           ->  [0, 3]   // a zero pair, not [i, i]
edgeCases: Duplicate values that form the answer ([3,3]).
Negative numbers.
The answer is never `[i, i]` — an element cannot be reused.
FOLLOW-UP
Can you come up with an algorithm that is less than O(n^2) time complexity?

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time, O(1) space — test every pair with nested loops.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(n) space — one pass, storing `value -> index` in a hash map and looking up `target - value`.

problems.title: Contains Duplicate
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if any value appears at least twice, and `false` if every element is distinct.
examples: containsDuplicate([-1, 0, 1, 2])  ->  false   // negatives and zero are distinct values
edgeCases: Single-element array — always false.
All elements identical.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time, O(1) space — compare every pair.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(n) space — insert into a Set and stop at the first collision.

problems.title: Product of Array Except Self
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `answer` where `answer[i]` is the product of all elements of `nums` except `nums[i]`. You must solve it WITHOUT using division, in O(n) time.
constraints: The product of any prefix or suffix fits in a 32-bit integer.
examples: productExceptSelf([0, 0])             ->  [0, 0]   // two zeros wipe everything out
edgeCases: A single zero — every slot except its own becomes 0.
Two or more zeros — the whole answer is 0.
FOLLOW-UP
Can you solve the problem in O(1) extra space complexity? (The output array does not count
as extra space.)

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — recompute the product for each index.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) extra space (output excluded) — a prefix pass then a suffix pass, accumulating into the result array.

problems.title: Maximum Subarray
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum. The subarray must contain at least one element.
examples: maxSubArray([0, -3, 0])                       ->  0   // best sum is 0, from a single 0
maxSubArray([2, -1, 2, -1, 2])                ->  4   // a dip is worth crossing
edgeCases: All numbers negative — the answer is the single largest element, not 0.
Single element.
FOLLOW-UP
If you have figured out the O(n) solution, try coding another solution using the divide and
conquer approach.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — sum every subarray.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — Kadane's algorithm: at each index keep the best sum ending here.

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.problem: Given an array of strings `strs`, group the anagrams together. Return the groups in any order; the strings inside a group may be in any order.
constraints: strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
examples: ->  [["ab","ba"], ["abc","cba","bac"]]   // groups and members may be in any order
groupAnagrams([""])            ->  [[""]]   // the empty string is its own group
groupAnagrams(["", "", "a"])   ->  [["", ""], ["a"]]   // equal empty strings group together
edgeCases: The empty string is its own group.
Single-character strings.

complexity.naive: O(n^2 * k) time — compare each string against every group.
complexity.target: O(n * k) time — key each string by a 26-slot character count (or its sorted form) in a hash map.

problems.title: Top K Frequent Elements
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k` most frequent elements. The answer may be returned in any order.
constraints: k is in the range [1, number of distinct elements]
The answer is guaranteed to be unique.
examples: topKFrequent([1, 2], 2)                ->  [1, 2]   // every value ties at count 1; any order
topKFrequent([-1, -1, 2, 2, 2, 3], 2)  ->  [2, -1]   // negatives are valid keys; any order
topKFrequent([1, 1, 2, 2, 3], 3)       ->  [1, 2, 3]   // k === number of distinct values
edgeCases: k equals the number of distinct elements — return them all.
All elements identical.
Negative values are valid keys.

complexity.naive: O(n log n) time — count, then sort every distinct value by frequency.
complexity.target: O(n) time — bucket sort by frequency (a frequency can never exceed n), or a size-k heap for O(n log k).

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.problem: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return true if `t` is an anagram of `s`. An anagram uses exactly the same characters with the same counts, reordered.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters.
examples: isAnagram("aacc", "ccac")        ->  false   // same letter set, different counts
edgeCases: Character COUNTS must match, not just the set of characters.
FOLLOW-UP
Follow-up: what changes for Unicode input?

complexity.naive: O(n log n) time — sort both strings and compare.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — a 26-slot count array incremented by s and decremented by t.

problems.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
problems.problem: Given an unsorted array `nums`, return the length of the longest sequence of consecutive integers in it. The elements need not be adjacent in the array. Must run in O(n) time.
constraints: Your solution must run in O(n) time.
examples: longestConsecutive([1, 2, 0, 1])                         ->  3   // the duplicate 1 does not inflate [0,1,2]
edgeCases: Empty array returns 0.
Duplicates must not inflate the count.

complexity.naive: O(n log n) time — sort and scan for runs. Correct, but misses the target.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(n) space — put everything in a Set, and only start counting from x when x-1 is absent, so each run is walked once.

problems.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the total number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals `k`.
examples: subarraySum([0, 0, 0], 0)                  ->  6   // every one of the 6 subarrays sums to 0
subarraySum([3, 4, 7, 2, -3, 1, 4, 2], 7)  ->  4   // negatives rule out a sliding window
edgeCases: Zeros create extra valid subarrays.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — sum every subarray with a running total.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(n) space — a prefix-sum frequency map: at each index add the count of previously seen `prefix - k`.

problems.title: Majority Element
problems.problem: Given an array `nums` of size n, return the element that appears more than n/2 times. You may assume a majority element always exists.
constraints: A majority element is guaranteed to exist.
edgeCases: A single element is trivially the majority.
'More than n/2' is strict — exactly half does not qualify.

complexity.naive: O(n) time, O(n) space — count every value in a hash map and take the largest count.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — Boyer-Moore voting: keep a candidate and a counter, resetting the candidate whenever the counter hits zero.

problems.title: Move Zeroes
problems.problem: Given an array `nums`, move all zeroes to the end while keeping the relative order of the non-zero elements. You must do this IN PLACE without copying the array.
constraints: You must do it in place, without making a copy of the array.
edgeCases: An array of all zeroes, or with no zeroes.
The order of the non-zero elements must be preserved.
FOLLOW-UP
Could you minimize the total number of operations done?

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — repeatedly find a zero and shift everything after it left by one.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — a write pointer for the next non-zero slot; after one pass, fill the tail with zeroes.

problems.title: Rotate Array
problems.problem: Given an array `nums`, rotate it to the right by `k` steps, where k is non-negative. Solve it in place with O(1) extra space.
examples: rotate([1, 2], k = 3)             ->  [2, 1]   // k exceeds the length
rotate([1], k = 0)                ->  [1]   // single element, no rotation
rotate([1, 2, 3, 4], k = 4)       ->  [1, 2, 3, 4]   // k === n is a full turn
edgeCases: k may be larger than the array length.
k = 0 leaves the array untouched.
FOLLOW-UP
An extra array is O(n) space and misses the target.
Could you do it in-place with O(1) extra space?

complexity.naive: O(n * k) time — rotate by one position, k times.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — the triple reversal trick: reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k, then reverse the rest.

problems.title: Contains Duplicate II
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return true if there are two DISTINCT indices i and j such that nums[i] == nums[j] and |i - j| <= k.
examples: containsNearbyDuplicate([1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3], 2)  ->  false   // duplicates exist, but too far apart
containsNearbyDuplicate([1, 1], 0)              ->  false   // k = 0 can never succeed
containsNearbyDuplicate([1, 2, 3, 1], 10)       ->  true   // k larger than the array
edgeCases: k = 0 can never succeed — the indices must be distinct.
k larger than the array length behaves like plain Contains Duplicate.

complexity.naive: O(n * k) time — for every index, scan the next k elements.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(min(n, k)) space — a sliding-window Set of the last k values (or a map of value -> last index seen).

problems.title: Isomorphic Strings
problems.problem: Two strings `s` and `t` are isomorphic if the characters in `s` can be replaced to get `t`. Every occurrence of a character must be replaced with the same character, preserving order. No two characters may map to the same character, but a character may map to itself. Return true if `s` and `t` are isomorphic.
constraints: s and t consist of any valid ASCII characters.
examples: isIsomorphic("foo", "bar")      ->  false   // 'o' would need to map to both 'a' and 'r'
isIsomorphic("badc", "baba")    ->  false   // 'd' and 'c' would both map to 'b'/'a' collisions
isIsomorphic("13:00", "24:11")  ->  true   // digits and punctuation are fine
edgeCases: The mapping must be one-to-one in BOTH directions: "badc" / "baba" is false.
Characters are not limited to letters (digits, spaces, punctuation).

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — for each pair of positions, check that equal-in-s means equal-in-t.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space (bounded alphabet) — two maps, s -> t and t -> s, checked on every step.

problems.title: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
problems.problem: Given an array `nums` of n integers where each nums[i] is in the range [1, n], return an array of all the integers in [1, n] that do not appear in `nums`. Any order is accepted.
examples: findDisappearedNumbers([3, 3, 3, 3])              ->  [1, 2, 4]   // all the same value; any order
edgeCases: Nothing missing (a permutation of 1..n) returns [].
Every slot holds the same value, so n - 1 numbers are missing.
FOLLOW-UP
Could you do it without extra space (the returned list does not count) in O(n) time?

complexity.naive: O(n) time, O(n) space — put every value in a Set, then check 1..n.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) extra space — for each value v, negate nums[|v| - 1]; indices that stay positive are the missing numbers.

problems.title: Majority Element II
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums` of size n, return all elements that appear MORE than n/3 times. Any order is accepted.
examples: majorityElement([1, 2, 3])           ->  []   // each hits exactly n/3, which is not MORE than n/3
majorityElement([2, 2, 1, 1, 3])     ->  [2, 1]   // the maximum of two answers; any order
edgeCases: There can be at most TWO such elements — and there may be none.
'More than n/3' is strict: exactly n/3 does not qualify.
FOLLOW-UP
Solve it in linear time and O(1) space. (See 101 Majority Element first.)

complexity.naive: O(n) time, O(n) space — count everything in a hash map.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — Boyer-Moore with two candidates and two counters, then a counting pass to confirm each candidate really exceeds n/3.

problems.title: Find All Duplicates in an Array
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums` of length n where every value is in [1, n] and each value appears ONCE or TWICE, return an array of all the values that appear twice. Any order is accepted.
constraints: Each element appears once or twice.
You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time and uses only constant extra space.
examples: findDuplicates([2, 1, 2, 1])              ->  [2, 1]   // every value duplicated; any order
edgeCases: No duplicates at all returns [].
Every value duplicated (n is even, n/2 answers).

complexity.naive: O(n) time, O(n) space — a Set of seen values.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) extra space — for each |v|, if nums[|v| - 1] is already negative, v is a duplicate; otherwise negate it.

problems.title: First Missing Positive
problems.problem: Given an unsorted integer array `nums`, return the smallest positive integer that is NOT present in `nums`. You must run in O(n) time and use O(1) auxiliary space.
examples: firstMissingPositive([7, 8, 9, 11, 12])  ->  1   // no small positives at all
firstMissingPositive([1, 2, 3])          ->  4   // 1..n all present, so the answer is n + 1
firstMissingPositive([2, 2, 1, 1])       ->  3   // duplicates do not fill the gap
edgeCases: Duplicates and negatives are allowed (unlike 089 Missing Number, so sum/XOR tricks fail).
If 1..n are all present, the answer is n + 1.

complexity.naive: O(n log n) time — sort, then walk looking for the first gap. Or O(n) time with a Set,
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — cyclic placement: swap each value v in [1, n] to index v - 1 until it is home, then the first index i with nums[i] != i + 1 gives i + 1.

problems.title: Longest Palindrome
problems.problem: Given a string `s` of lowercase and uppercase letters, return the length of the longest palindrome that can be BUILT from those letters (each letter used at most as many times as it appears). Letters are case sensitive: "Aa" is not a palindrome.
constraints: s consists of lowercase and/or uppercase English letters only.
examples: longestPalindrome("Aa")        ->  1   // case sensitive — no pair here
longestPalindrome("abc")       ->  1   // no pairs; one odd letter sits in the middle
edgeCases: A letter with an odd count still contributes count - 1 letters.
At most ONE odd-count letter can sit in the middle.

complexity.naive: Trying arrangements is exponential; there is no reason to.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space (52 letters) — count letters, add every even part, and add 1 if any count was odd.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome
problems.problem: Given a string `s`, return `true` if it is a palindrome after converting all uppercase letters to lowercase and removing every non-alphanumeric character.
constraints: s consists of printable ASCII characters.
examples: isPalindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")  ->  true
isPalindrome(".,")                              ->  true   // no alphanumeric characters at all
isPalindrome("0P")                              ->  false   // '0' and 'p' are both alphanumeric, but differ
edgeCases: A string with no alphanumeric characters is a palindrome.
Mixed case.
Digits count as alphanumeric.

complexity.naive: O(n) time, O(n) space — build a cleaned string, then compare it to its reverse.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — two pointers walking inward, skipping non-alphanumeric characters in place.

problems.title: 3Sum
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums`, return all unique triplets `[nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]` with distinct indices such that they sum to zero. The solution set must not contain duplicate triplets.
examples: threeSum([1, 2, 3])              ->  []   // smallest input, no triplet sums to 0
threeSum([-1, -1, 2, 2, 0, 0])   ->  [[-1, -1, 2]]   // duplicates collapse to one triplet
edgeCases: Duplicate triplets must be filtered out — this is the hard part.
Fewer than three elements.
All zeros.

complexity.naive: O(n^3) time — three nested loops plus a de-duplication pass.
complexity.target: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space — sort, then for each index run a two-pointer scan, skipping repeated values at every level.

problems.title: Container With Most Water
problems.problem: Given an integer array `height` where each value is a vertical line at that index, find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container holding the most water. Return the maximum area. You may not slant the container.
examples: maxArea([0, 2])                       ->  0   // a zero-height line holds nothing
maxArea([1, 2, 1])                    ->  2   // the two outer 1s beat any taller-but-closer pair
edgeCases: Zero-height lines contribute no area.
Exactly two lines.
Area is min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l), not the sum.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — evaluate every pair of lines.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — two pointers at the ends, always moving the shorter line inward.

problems.title: Trapping Rain Water
problems.problem: Given `n` non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much rain water can be trapped after raining.
examples: trap([5])                        ->  0   // a single bar has no walls
trap([0, 3, 0, 2, 0, 4])         ->  7   // leading zero wasted; 3 + 1 + 3 trapped inside
edgeCases: Monotonic arrays trap zero water.
Leading and trailing zeros.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — for each bar scan left and right for its tallest neighbor.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — two pointers tracking `leftMax` and `rightMax`, always advancing the smaller side.

problems.title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
problems.problem: Given a sorted array `nums`, remove the duplicates IN PLACE so each unique element appears once, keeping the relative order. Return `k`, the number of unique elements; the first k slots of nums must hold them. What is left beyond k does not matter.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.
You must do it in place with O(1) extra memory.
examples: removeDuplicates([1, 2, 3])                ->  3, nums starts [1, 2, 3]   // no duplicates to remove
edgeCases: A single element.
All elements identical — the answer is 1.

complexity.naive: O(n) time, O(n) space — build a fresh array of uniques, which the constraint forbids.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — a slow write pointer and a fast read pointer; write only when the value differs from the last written one.

problems.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
problems.problem: Given a 1-indexed array `numbers` sorted in non-decreasing order, find two numbers that add up to `target` and return their 1-based indices [index1, index2] with index1 < index2. You must use O(1) extra space.
constraints: Exactly one solution exists; numbers is sorted ascending.
You must use only constant extra space.
examples: twoSum([1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 9, 56, 90], 8)  ->  [4, 5]   // the pair is two equal values
edgeCases: The answer is 1-indexed — a classic off-by-one trap.
Negative values.

complexity.naive: O(n) time, O(n) space — the hash map from Two Sum, which violates the O(1) space
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — two pointers at the ends; move left in when the sum is too small, right in when too large.

problems.title: Sort Colors
problems.problem: Given an array `nums` with n objects colored 0 (red), 1 (white) or 2 (blue), sort them IN PLACE so equal colors are adjacent in the order 0, 1, 2. You may not use a library sort, and should do it in one pass.
edgeCases: An array of a single color.
Already-sorted input.

complexity.naive: O(n) two-pass counting sort — count each color, then overwrite. Correct, but two
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space, one pass — the Dutch National Flag algorithm with low/mid/high pointers.

problems.title: Valid Palindrome II
problems.problem: Given a string `s`, return true if `s` can be a palindrome after deleting AT MOST one character from it.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
examples: validPalindrome("aaaa")     ->  true   // all-same, no deletion needed
validPalindrome("cuppucu")  ->  true   // only deleting the RIGHT side works
edgeCases: At the first mismatch you may have to try BOTH deletions: skipping the left character can
fail where skipping the right one succeeds ("cuppucu").
A single character is a palindrome.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — delete each character in turn and check the remainder.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — two pointers; at the first mismatch, check whether s[l+1..r] or s[l..r-1] is a palindrome.

problems.title: Squares of a Sorted Array
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, return an array of the squares of each number, also sorted in non-decreasing order.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.
examples: sortedSquares([-3, -2, -1])        ->  [1, 4, 9]   // all negative: squares reverse the order
sortedSquares([1, 2, 3])           ->  [1, 4, 9]   // all non-negative: order is kept
sortedSquares([-2, -1, 1, 2])      ->  [1, 1, 4, 4]   // mirrored values square to duplicates
edgeCases: All negative: the squares come out in reverse order.
All non-negative: already in order.
FOLLOW-UP
Squaring then sorting is O(n log n). Can you find an O(n) solution?

complexity.naive: O(n log n) time — square everything, then sort.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(n) space for the output — pointers at both ends; place the larger square at the back of the result and move that pointer inward.

problems.title: Is Subsequence
problems.problem: Given two strings `s` and `t`, return true if `s` is a subsequence of `t`: it can be formed by deleting some (possibly zero) characters of `t` without changing the order of the rest.
constraints: s and t consist only of lowercase English letters.
examples: isSubsequence("", "abc")        ->  true   // the empty string is a subsequence of anything
isSubsequence("abc", "ab")      ->  false   // s longer than t can never match
edgeCases: s longer than t can never match.
Order matters: "ba" is not a subsequence of "abc".
FOLLOW-UP
If there are many incoming s strings (say 10^9) against the same t, how would you change
your approach?

complexity.naive: Exponential — generate subsequences of t and compare.
complexity.target: O(|t|) time, O(1) space — one pointer in each string; advance the s pointer only on a match. (Follow-up: per-letter index lists of t plus binary search.)

problems.title: Reverse String
problems.problem: Write a function that reverses an array of characters `s` IN PLACE. Do not return anything; modify `s` directly using O(1) extra memory.
constraints: s[i] is a printable ASCII character.
examples: reverseString(["a"])                           ->  s becomes ["a"]   // single character, unchanged
reverseString(["x", "y", "z"])                 ->  s becomes ["z", "y", "x"]   // odd length: the middle stays put
reverseString(["7", "7", "7"])                 ->  s becomes ["7", "7", "7"]   // all same, visibly unchanged
edgeCases: A single character is unchanged.
Odd length: the middle character stays put.

complexity.naive: O(n) time, O(n) space — build a reversed copy and write it back (breaks the rule).
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — swap s[l] and s[r], moving both pointers inward.

problems.title: 3Sum Closest
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums` of length n and an integer `target`, find three integers at distinct indices whose sum is closest to `target`. Return that SUM.
constraints: Each input has exactly one closest sum.
examples: threeSumClosest([1, 1, 1], 0)                        ->  3   // smallest input; closest sum is above the target
threeSumClosest([-1000, -1000, -1000], 10000)        ->  -3000   // the only sum, far below the target
threeSumClosest([4, 0, 5, -5, 3, 3, 0, -4, -5], -2)  ->  -2   // exact match with duplicates around
edgeCases: An exact match can stop the search early.
The closest sum may be above or below the target.

complexity.naive: O(n^3) time — try every triple.
complexity.target: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space — sort; fix i, then two pointers on the rest, moving left when the sum is too small and right when too large.

problems.title: 4Sum
problems.problem: Given an array `nums` of n integers, return all UNIQUE quadruplets [nums[a], nums[b], nums[c], nums[d]] with distinct indices a, b, c, d whose sum equals `target`. The quadruplets and the numbers inside them may be in any order.
examples: fourSum([1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2], 6)  ->  [[1, 1, 2, 2]]   // heavy duplicates, still one result
edgeCases: Fewer than four elements returns [].
Heavy duplicates must not produce repeated quadruplets.

complexity.naive: O(n^4) time — every quadruple, deduplicated with a Set of sorted keys.
complexity.target: O(n^3) time, O(1) extra space — sort; two nested loops fix a and b, then two pointers find c and d, skipping equal neighbours.

problems.title: Boats to Save People
problems.problem: `people[i]` is the weight of person i, and every boat can carry at most `limit` weight. Each boat carries AT MOST TWO people at once, provided their total weight is <= limit. Return the minimum number of boats needed to carry everyone.
examples: numRescueBoats([1, 1, 1, 1], 4)  ->  2   // all four fit by weight, but two per boat is the cap
edgeCases: Someone weighing exactly `limit` always rides alone.
Two people is the cap even when three would fit under the limit.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — for each person, search for the best remaining partner.
complexity.target: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space — sort; the heaviest boards every boat, taking the lightest along whenever the pair fits.

problems.title: Next Permutation
problems.problem: Rearrange `nums` IN PLACE into the next lexicographically greater permutation. If no greater permutation exists (the array is in descending order), rearrange it into the lowest possible order (ascending). Use only O(1) extra memory and return nothing.
examples: nextPermutation([1])        ->  nums becomes [1]   // a single element is unchanged
nextPermutation([5, 5, 5])  ->  nums becomes [5, 5, 5]   // all same: already the lowest order
nextPermutation([1, 3, 2])  ->  nums becomes [2, 1, 3]   // pivot at index 0, suffix reversed
edgeCases: Duplicate values: swap with the rightmost element STRICTLY greater than the pivot.
A single element is unchanged.

complexity.naive: O(n! * n) time — generate all permutations in sorted order and find the next one.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — find pivot i, swap it with the rightmost larger element, then reverse the suffix after i with two pointers.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

problems.title: Minimum Window Substring

problems.title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement

problems.title: Sliding Window Maximum

problems.title: Min Stack
problems.problem: Design a stack supporting push, pop, top and retrieving the minimum element, EVERY operation in O(1) time. Implement the MinStack class with push(val), pop(), top() and getMin().
constraints: pop, top and getMin are only called on a non-empty stack.
getMin must run in O(1) time.
new MinStack()             initialize an empty stack
push(val)       -> void    push val onto the stack
pop()           -> void    remove the element on top of the stack
top()           -> number  return the element on top of the stack
getMin()        -> number  return the minimum element currently in the stack
examples: a.top()  ->  5;  a.getMin()          ->  5    // one element is both top and min
const b = new MinStack(); b.push(2); b.push(2); b.push(1); b.pop();
b.getMin()                           ->  2    // a duplicated min must survive one pop
const c = new MinStack(); c.push(3); c.push(1); c.pop(); c.push(4);
c.getMin()                           ->  3    // popping the min restores the previous one
const d = new MinStack(); d.push(7); d.push(7); d.push(7); d.pop();
one.top()  ->  7;  one.getMin()  ->  7    // single element: top is also the min
dup.pop(); dup.pop(); dup.getMin()  ->  2  // duplicate minimum survives one pop
asc.getMin()  ->  1                        // min stays at the bottom, never on top
neg.pop(); neg.getMin()  ->  0             // popping the min restores the previous one
edgeCases: Duplicate minimums must survive a single pop.
Negative values.

complexity.naive: O(n) getMin — scan the whole stack on every call.
complexity.target: O(1) for every operation — keep a parallel stack (or store [val, minSoFar] pairs) so each entry carries the minimum beneath it.

get(key, timestamp)         -> string  return the value at the largest stored timestamp <=

complexity.target: O(m * n) time, O(n) space — dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1], reducible to a single rolling row.

problems.title: Decode Ways
problems.problem: A message of digits was encoded with 'A' -> "1" ... 'Z' -> "26". Given a string `s` of digits, return the number of ways to decode it. The answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
constraints: s contains only digits and may contain leading zeros.
examples: numDecodings("06")     ->  0   // a leading zero is invalid
numDecodings("27")     ->  1   // only "BG" — 27 is out of range
edgeCases: '0' alone is never decodable; only "10" and "20" are valid pairs containing it.
Two-digit codes must be between 10 and 26 inclusive.
A string starting with '0' decodes zero ways.

complexity.naive: O(2^n) time — recurse on taking one or two digits without memoisation.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — dp[i] = dp[i-1] (if the single digit is valid) + dp[i-2] (if the pair is 10..26).

problems.title: Maximum Product Subarray
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums`, find the contiguous subarray with the largest product and return that product.
constraints: Every prefix or suffix product fits in a 32-bit integer.
examples: maxProduct([-2, 3, -4])       ->  24    // two negatives make a positive
edgeCases: Zeros reset the running product.
A single negative element is its own answer.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — multiply out every subarray.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — Kadane's variant carrying both the running max and min, swapping them on a negative value.

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
problems.problem: Given a string `s`, return the longest palindromic substring in it. If several are tied, any one of them is acceptable.
constraints: s consists of digits and English letters.
examples: longestPalindrome("ac")                ->  "a"      // any single char is acceptable
edgeCases: Single characters are palindromes.
No palindrome longer than 1 means returning any single character.

complexity.naive: O(n^3) time — check every substring for palindromicity.
complexity.target: O(n^2) time, O(1) space — expand around each of the 2n - 1 possible centers. (Manacher's algorithm reaches O(n).)

problems.title: House Robber II
problems.problem: The houses are arranged in a CIRCLE, so the first and last are adjacent. You cannot rob two adjacent houses. Return the maximum you can rob.
examples: rob([2, 3, 2])          ->  3     // cannot take both 2s, they are adjacent
rob([2, 7])             ->  7     // two houses — take the larger
rob([1, 3, 1, 3, 100])  ->  103   // houses 1 and 4 are not adjacent
edgeCases: A single house — the circle rule cannot apply.
Two houses — take the larger.
The first and last houses can never BOTH be robbed.

complexity.naive: O(2^n) time — enumerate every subset and reject adjacent picks, now including the
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — run the linear House Robber twice, once excluding the last house and once excluding the first, and take the better.

problems.title: Coin Change II
problems.problem: Given an array of distinct coin denominations and a target `amount`, return the number of distinct COMBINATIONS that make up that amount. Coins are unlimited. Order does not matter: 1+2 and 2+1 are the same combination.
edgeCases: Amount 0 has exactly one combination — take nothing.
Order does NOT matter; counting permutations is the classic wrong answer.

complexity.naive: O(amount^coins) time — recurse over every sequence of coin choices, which counts
complexity.target: O(coins * amount) time, O(amount) space — a 1-D DP where the coin loop is outermost, so each combination is counted once.

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.problem: Given an array `nums` of positive integers, determine whether it can be split into two subsets whose sums are equal.
examples: canPartition([2])            ->  false   // a single element cannot be split
canPartition([1, 2, 5])      ->  false   // sum 8 is even, yet no half exists
edgeCases: An odd total sum is immediately false.
A single element cannot be split.

complexity.naive: O(2^n) time — enumerate every subset and compare sums.
complexity.target: O(n * sum) time, O(sum) space — a boolean DP over reachable sums up to total/2, iterating the inner loop DOWNWARD so each number is used once.

problems.title: Target Sum
problems.problem: Given an array `nums` and an integer `target`, put a '+' or '-' before each number and concatenate them into an expression. Return how many assignments evaluate to target.
examples: findTargetSumWays([1, 2, 3, 4], 11)    ->  0   // target beyond the total sum
edgeCases: Zeros double the count — +0 and -0 are distinct assignments.
A target beyond the total sum is unreachable.
Every element must get a sign; none may be skipped.

complexity.naive: O(2^n) time — try both signs at every index without memoisation.
complexity.target: O(n * sum) time — memoise on (index, runningSum), or transform it into a subset-sum: find subsets totalling (sum + target) / 2.

problems.title: Burst Balloons
problems.problem: Balloons hold coins in `nums`. Bursting balloon i earns nums[i-1] * nums[i] * nums[i+1] coins, where out-of-range neighbors count as 1, and its neighbors then become adjacent. Return the maximum coins obtainable by bursting all balloons.
edgeCases: A single balloon earns 1 * nums[0] * 1.

complexity.naive: O(n!) time — try every bursting order.
complexity.target: O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space — interval DP over (left, right) ranges, choosing the last balloon burst inside each range.

problems.title: Subsets
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums` of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). The solution must not contain duplicate subsets; any order is fine.
examples: subsets([-1])          ->  [[], [-1]]   // one element still yields the empty subset
edgeCases: The empty subset is always included.
There are exactly 2^n subsets.

complexity.naive: There is no polynomial solution — the output alone is 2^n.
complexity.target: O(n * 2^n) time — backtracking (include/exclude at each index), or iterate the bitmask 0..2^n - 1.

problems.title: Permutations
problems.problem: Given an array `nums` of distinct integers, return all possible permutations in any order.
examples: permute([1, 2, 3, 4])  ->  24 permutations   // exactly n! of them
edgeCases: A single element yields one permutation.
There are exactly n! results.

complexity.naive: Generating candidates randomly until all n! are found is unbounded.
complexity.target: O(n * n!) time — backtracking with a used-set, or swapping elements in place.

problems.title: N-Queens
problems.problem: Place `n` queens on an n x n chessboard so that no two attack each other. Return all distinct solutions, each as a list of strings where 'Q' is a queen and '.' is empty.
examples: solveNQueens(8)  ->  92 distinct solutions   // the classic board
edgeCases: n = 2 and n = 3 have no solutions.
n = 1 has exactly one.

complexity.naive: O(n^n) time — try every square for every queen and validate at the end.
complexity.target: Backtracking with column and two diagonal sets, pruning invalid placements immediately — roughly O(n!) with heavy pruning.

problems.title: Generate Parentheses
problems.problem: Given `n` pairs of parentheses, generate all combinations of well-formed parentheses.
examples: generateParenthesis(8)  ->  1430 strings   // the largest allowed n
edgeCases: Every result has exactly 2n characters.
The count of results is the nth Catalan number.

complexity.naive: O(2^(2n) * n) time — generate every string of brackets and filter the valid ones.
complexity.target: O(4^n / sqrt(n)) time — backtrack, only ever adding '(' while open < n and ')' while close < open, so invalid branches are never built.

problems.title: Combination Sum
problems.problem: Given an array of DISTINCT integers `candidates` and a `target`, return all unique combinations summing to target. Each candidate may be used unlimited times. Two combinations are the same if they contain the same numbers with the same counts.
examples: combinationSum([2, 4], 7)        ->  []   // even candidates never sum to an odd target
edgeCases: Candidates may repeat within one combination.
[2,2,3] and [2,3,2] are the SAME combination.
No valid combination returns an empty array.

complexity.naive: Recursing over all candidates at every level generates permutations, then needs de-
complexity.target: Backtracking with a start index and a remaining target, pruning as soon as remaining goes negative.

problems.title: Word Search
problems.problem: Given an m x n grid of characters and a string `word`, return true if the word can be built from sequentially adjacent cells (horizontal or vertical neighbors). The same cell may not be used more than once.
constraints: board and word consist of English letters.
examples: exist([["A","B"],["C","D"]], "ABD")    ->  true   // A -> B then down to D
exist([["A","B"],["C","D"]], "AD")     ->  false   // A and D are only diagonal
exist([["A","A"],["A","A"]], "AAAAA")  ->  false   // longer than the cell count
edgeCases: A cell cannot be reused within one path.
Diagonal moves are not allowed.
A word longer than the cell count is immediately false.

complexity.naive: Trying every cell sequence without pruning is factorial in the grid size.
complexity.target: O(m * n * 4^L) time — DFS from every matching start cell, marking visited cells and restoring them on the way out.

problems.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
problems.problem: Given a string of digits 2-9, return all letter combinations the number could spell, using the standard telephone keypad mapping. Any order is acceptable.
examples: letterCombinations("2345")  ->  81 strings   // the longest allowed input
edgeCases: The empty string returns an empty array, NOT [""].
7 (pqrs) and 9 (wxyz) map to four letters, the rest to three.
1 and 0 never appear in the input.

complexity.naive: There is no polynomial approach — the output itself is up to 4^n entries.
complexity.target: O(4^n * n) time — backtracking over one digit per level, appending each mapped letter.

problems.title: Subsets II
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums` that MAY CONTAIN DUPLICATES, return all possible subsets without any duplicate subsets. Any order is acceptable.
examples: subsetsWithDup([1, 2])     ->  [[], [1], [1,2], [2]]   // no duplicates, so the full 2^n
subsetsWithDup([0, 0, 0])  ->  [[], [0], [0,0], [0,0,0]]   // all equal, only n+1 subsets
edgeCases: Duplicates in the input must not produce duplicate subsets.
The result count is below 2^n whenever duplicates exist.

complexity.naive: Generating all 2^n subsets and de-duplicating via string keys works but wastes time
complexity.target: O(n * 2^n) time — sort, then backtrack skipping any value equal to its predecessor at the same recursion depth.

problems.title: Combination Sum II
problems.problem: Given a collection `candidates` that may contain duplicates and a `target`, find all unique combinations summing to target. Each candidate may be used AT MOST ONCE.
examples: combinationSum2([2], 1)                 ->  []   // no combination reaches the target
edgeCases: Each element is usable once, but equal VALUES may legitimately appear twice (as [1,1,6]
shows).
No solution returns an empty array.

complexity.naive: Enumerating all subsets and filtering by sum is O(2^n) with a costly de-duplication
complexity.target: Backtracking on a sorted array: advance the index by one each level (single use) and skip a value equal to its predecessor within the same loop.

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning
problems.problem: Given a string `s`, partition it so every substring in the partition is a palindrome. Return all possible palindrome partitionings.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.
edgeCases: Single characters are always palindromes, so a partitioning always exists.
Cuts must cover the whole string with no gaps.

complexity.naive: O(n * 2^n) time — generate every partitioning and validate each part afterwards.
complexity.target: Backtracking that only recurses when the current prefix is already a palindrome, optionally with an O(n^2) precomputed palindrome table.

problems.title: Merge Intervals
problems.problem: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [start, end], merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping intervals covering all the input.
examples: merge([[1,4]])                       ->  [[1,4]]         // single interval, nothing to merge
merge([[1,4],[0,4]])                 ->  [[0,4]]         // shared end, later start comes first
edgeCases: Intervals touching at an endpoint merge.
One interval fully inside another.
The input is not sorted.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — repeatedly scan for any overlapping pair until none remain.
complexity.target: O(n log n) time — sort by start, then sweep, extending the current interval whenever the next start is <= the current end.

problems.title: Jump Game
problems.problem: You are given an array `nums` where nums[i] is the maximum jump length from index i. Starting at index 0, return true if you can reach the last index.
examples: canJump([0])              ->  true    // already at the end
canJump([2, 0, 0])        ->  true    // one jump clears both zeros
canJump([1, 0, 1, 0])     ->  false   // the first 0 is a dead end
edgeCases: A single element — you are already there.
A leading 0 with length > 1 is immediately stuck.
Jumps may be shorter than the maximum.

complexity.naive: O(2^n) time — recurse over every possible jump length from each index.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — greedily track the furthest reachable index; fail the moment i exceeds it.

problems.title: Non-overlapping Intervals
problems.problem: Given an array of intervals, return the minimum number you must remove so that the rest are non-overlapping.
examples: eraseOverlapIntervals([[1,2]])                     ->  0   // a single interval never overlaps
edgeCases: Intervals that only touch at an endpoint do not overlap.
Identical duplicate intervals.

complexity.naive: O(2^n) time — try every subset and keep the largest compatible one.
complexity.target: O(n log n) time — sort by END, then greedily keep every interval starting at or after the last kept end.

problems.title: Insert Interval
problems.problem: Given a list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start, insert a new interval and merge where necessary. Return the resulting sorted, non-overlapping list.
constraints: intervals is sorted by start and non-overlapping.
examples: insert([[3,5]], [1,2])                             ->  [[1,2],[3,5]]   // goes before all, no overlap
insert([[1,5]], [6,8])                             ->  [[1,5],[6,8]]   // goes after all, no overlap
insert([[1,2],[5,6]], [2,5])                       ->  [[1,6]]         // touches both ends, all merge
edgeCases: An empty input list.
The new interval may go before all, after all, or swallow several.
Touching endpoints ([1,2] and [2,3]) merge.

complexity.naive: O(n log n) time — append the interval, re-sort, and run a full merge pass.
complexity.target: O(n) time — the input is already sorted, so emit everything ending before the new start, merge the overlapping run, then emit the rest.

problems.title: Gas Station
problems.problem: There are n gas stations in a circle. gas[i] is the fuel available at station i, and cost[i] the fuel needed to reach station i+1. Starting with an empty tank, return the index you must begin at to travel the circuit once, or -1 if it is impossible. If a solution exists it is unique.
examples: canCompleteCircuit([3,1,1], [1,2,2])          ->  0    // the tank never dips below 0
edgeCases: If total gas < total cost, no start works — return -1.
The tank starts empty and may never go negative mid-journey.
The route wraps around the end of the array.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — simulate a full circuit from every possible starting station.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — one pass: if the running tank goes negative at i, no station up to i can be the start, so restart from i + 1.

problems.title: Partition Labels
problems.problem: Given a string `s`, partition it into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part. Return a list of the part sizes, in order. The parts concatenated in order must reconstruct s.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
examples: partitionLabels("aa")                        ->  [2]         // a repeat forces one part
edgeCases: A single character gives [1].
One letter spanning the whole string forces a single part.
The sizes must sum to s.length.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — for each candidate cut, verify no letter straddles it.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(26) space — record each letter's LAST index, then sweep, closing a part when the cursor reaches the running maximum last-index.

problems.title: Single Number
problems.problem: Given a non-empty array where every element appears twice except for one, find that single element. Must run in O(n) time using O(1) extra space.
constraints: Every element appears twice except one.
You must use only constant extra space.
examples: singleNumber([5, -3, 5])       ->  -3   // the loner may be negative
edgeCases: A single-element array.
Negative numbers.

complexity.naive: O(n) time but O(n) space — count occurrences in a map.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — XOR every element: pairs cancel to 0 and the loner survives.

problems.title: Counting Bits
problems.problem: Given an integer `n`, return an array of length n + 1 where ans[i] is the number of 1-bits in the binary representation of i.
examples: countBits(8)  ->  [0, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1]   // powers of two drop back to 1
edgeCases: n = 0 returns [0].
The result has n + 1 entries, not n.

complexity.naive: O(n log n) time — count the bits of each number independently.
complexity.target: O(n) time — DP: ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1), reusing the already-computed half.

problems.title: Reverse Integer
problems.problem: Given a signed 32-bit integer `x`, return x with its digits reversed. If reversing causes the value to fall outside [-2^31, 2^31 - 1], return 0.
edgeCases: Trailing zeros disappear.
Negative numbers keep their sign.
Overflow must be detected BEFORE it happens, not after.

complexity.naive: Reversing the string form and parsing it ignores the overflow requirement.
complexity.target: O(log x) time, O(1) space — pop digits with %10 and push with *10, checking against the 32-bit bound before each push.

problems.title: Pow(x, n)
problems.problem: Implement pow(x, n), which computes x raised to the power n. `n` may be negative.
examples: myPow(2.00000, 0)            ->  1.00000    // any x to the 0 is 1
myPow(-2.00000, 3)           ->  -8.00000   // a negative base keeps its sign
edgeCases: n = 0 returns 1 for any x.
Negative n means the reciprocal.
n = -2^31 overflows when negated — widen it first.

complexity.naive: O(n) time — multiply x by itself n times. With n = 2^31 that never finishes.
complexity.target: O(log n) time — fast exponentiation by squaring: x^n = (x^(n/2))^2, times x when n is odd.

problems.title: Rotate Image
problems.problem: Given an n x n 2D matrix representing an image, rotate it 90 degrees clockwise. You must rotate it IN PLACE — do not allocate another matrix.
constraints: You must rotate the matrix in place, without allocating another one.
edgeCases: A 1x1 matrix is unchanged.
Even and odd n both work with the transpose approach.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space — write into a fresh matrix, which the constraint forbids.
complexity.target: O(n^2) time, O(1) space — transpose the matrix, then reverse each row. (Anticlockwise: transpose, then reverse each column.)

problems.title: Number of 1 Bits
problems.problem: Write a function that takes an unsigned integer and returns its Hamming weight: the number of 1 bits in its binary representation.
constraints: The input is a 32-bit unsigned integer.
edgeCases: Zero has weight 0.
In JS, bitwise operators coerce to a SIGNED 32-bit integer.
All-ones input gives 32.
FOLLOW-UP
If this function is called many times, how would you optimize it?

complexity.naive: O(32) time — shift through all 32 positions regardless of how few bits are set.
complexity.target: O(number of set bits) time — n &= (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit each iteration, so the loop runs only as many times as there are 1s.

problems.title: Missing Number
problems.problem: Given an array `nums` containing n distinct numbers drawn from the range [0, n], return the one number in that range that is missing. Aim for O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
examples: missingNumber([0, 1])               ->  2   // the missing one can be n itself
missingNumber([0])                  ->  1   // n = 1, the top of the range is gone
missingNumber([1])                  ->  0   // n = 1, 0 is the one missing
edgeCases: The missing value may be 0 or n, at either end of the range.
FOLLOW-UP
A Set solution is O(n) space and misses the target.

complexity.naive: O(n log n) time — sort and find the first index-value mismatch.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — either XOR all indices with all values, or subtract the array sum from n(n+1)/2.

problems.title: Plus One
problems.problem: You are given a large integer as an array of digits, most significant digit first, with no leading zeros. Increment it by one and return the resulting digit array.
examples: plusOne([0])           ->  [1]         // the only legal leading zero
plusOne([9])           ->  [1, 0]      // a single 9 grows the array
edgeCases: All nines grows the array by one digit.
[0] becomes [1].
Converting to a Number overflows for 100 digits.

complexity.naive: Joining to a number, adding 1, and splitting back loses precision beyond 15 digits.
complexity.target: O(n) time — walk from the last digit: a digit below 9 increments and returns; a 9 becomes 0 and carries. If the loop ends still carrying, prepend a 1.

problems.title: Reverse Bits
problems.problem: Reverse the bits of a given 32-bit unsigned integer and return the result.
constraints: The input is a 32-bit unsigned integer.
examples: reverseBits(1)           ->  2147483648   // the lowest bit moves to the top
reverseBits(4294967295)  ->  4294967295   // all ones is its own reverse
edgeCases: Leading zeros matter — always process exactly 32 bits.
In JS, bitwise operations are signed.
FOLLOW-UP
Follow-up: how would you optimize for many repeated calls? (byte-level lookup table)

complexity.naive: Converting to a binary string, reversing it, and parsing back works but allocates on
complexity.target: O(32) time, O(1) space — shift the result left and push in the input's lowest bit, 32 times.

problems.title: Sum of Two Integers
problems.problem: Given two integers `a` and `b`, return their sum WITHOUT using the + or - operators.
edgeCases: Negative operands must work — two's complement handles this naturally.

complexity.naive: There is no simpler correct approach — the constraint is the whole exercise.
complexity.target: O(1) time (at most 32 iterations) — repeatedly combine the XOR sum with the shifted AND carry until no carry remains.

problems.title: Last Stone Weight
problems.problem: You repeatedly smash the two heaviest stones together. If they are equal both are destroyed; otherwise the heavier one is left with the weight difference. Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if none remain.
examples: lastStoneWeight([1, 1, 1])           ->  1   // a tie cancels, leaving one
edgeCases: A single stone survives untouched.
All stones may cancel out, giving 0.
The difference stone re-enters the pool and may be smashed again.

complexity.naive: O(n^2 log n) time — re-sort the array after every smash.
complexity.target: O(n log n) time — a max-heap: pop two, push back the difference when non-zero.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the kth largest element. This is the kth largest in sorted ORDER, not the kth distinct element.
examples: findKthLargest([3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], 6)           ->  1    // k = n is the minimum
edgeCases: Duplicates count separately — this is positional, not distinct.
k = 1 is the maximum; k = n is the minimum.
FOLLOW-UP
Sorting works but is not the intended complexity.

complexity.naive: O(n log n) time — sort descending and index k - 1.
complexity.target: O(n log k) with a size-k min-heap, or O(n) average with Quickselect (partition and recurse into one side only).

problems.title: K Closest Points to Origin
problems.problem: Given an array of points on the plane and an integer `k`, return the k points closest to the origin (0, 0) by Euclidean distance. Any order is acceptable.
examples: kClosest([[1, 3], [-2, 2]], 2)           ->  [[-2, 2], [1, 3]]   // k = n returns everything, any order
kClosest([[1, 0], [0, 1]], 1)            ->  [[1, 0]]            // a tie — either point is acceptable
edgeCases: k equal to the point count returns everything.
Negative coordinates are fine — squaring handles the sign.

complexity.naive: O(n log n) time — sort every point by distance when only k are needed.
complexity.target: O(n log k) with a size-k max-heap, or O(n) average with Quickselect on squared distance.

problems.title: Find Median from Data Stream
problems.problem: Design a data structure supporting addNum(num) to ingest a stream of integers and findMedian() to return the median of everything seen so far. Implement the MedianFinder class.
constraints: findMedian is only called after at least one addNum.
new MedianFinder()             initialize an empty stream
addNum(num)         -> void    add num to the stream
findMedian()        -> number  return the median of everything added so far
examples: mf.addNum(4);  mf.findMedian()  ->  2.5   // even count averages 2 and 3
one.addNum(6); one.findMedian()  ->  6.0   // a single number is its own median
dup.findMedian()                 ->  2.0   // duplicates are kept, not collapsed
one.addNum(7);  one.findMedian()  ->  7.0   // a single element is its own median
edgeCases: An even count averages the two middle values and may return a non-integer.
A single element is its own median.

complexity.naive: O(n log n) per query — keep an array and sort it on each findMedian call.
complexity.target: O(log n) insert, O(1) query — two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper, kept balanced within one element.

problems.title: Task Scheduler
problems.problem: Given an array of CPU `tasks` labelled A-Z and a cooldown `n`, identical tasks must be separated by at least n intervals. Each task takes one interval, and the CPU may idle. Return the minimum number of intervals needed to finish all tasks.
constraints: tasks[i] is an uppercase English letter.
examples: leastInterval(["A","A","A","B","B","B"], 2)  ->  8   // A B idle A B idle A B
leastInterval(["A","A","B","B"], 2)          ->  5   // a tie for most frequent shrinks idling
edgeCases: n = 0 means the answer is simply the task count.
The answer is never below the total number of tasks.

complexity.naive: Simulating interval by interval with a scan for the best available task is O(total *
complexity.target: O(n) time — either a max-heap with a cooldown queue, or the closed form: max(tasks.length, (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + countOfMaxFreq).

problems.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
problems.problem: Implement a trie supporting insert(word), search(word) returning whether the exact word was inserted, and startsWith(prefix) returning whether any inserted word has that prefix.
constraints: All inputs consist of lowercase English letters.
new Trie()                      initialize an empty trie
insert(word)        -> void     insert word into the trie
search(word)        -> boolean  return true if word was inserted before
startsWith(prefix)  -> boolean  return true if any inserted word begins with prefix
examples: t.search("app")        ->  false   // inserted as a prefix only
t.startsWith("apple")  ->  true    // a word is a prefix of itself
t.insert("app"); t.insert("app");  // a duplicate insert is harmless
edgeCases: search must distinguish a full word from a mere prefix.
Inserting the same word twice is harmless.
The empty prefix matches anything (if permitted by constraints).

complexity.naive: Storing words in an array makes startsWith O(n * L) per query.

problems.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure

examples: d.search("...")   ->  true    // all wildcards, and length 3 matches

A search string longer than any stored word is false.
A word may be entirely wildcards.

problems.title: Word Search II
problems.problem: Given an m x n board of characters and a list of words, return all words from the list that can be formed from sequentially adjacent cells (horizontal or vertical). A cell may not be reused within a single word.

complexity.target: Build a trie of ALL words, then DFS the board ONCE, walking the trie in step and abandoning a path the moment no trie node matches.

problems.title: Longest Common Prefix
problems.problem: Write a function to find the longest common prefix string among an array of strings. If there is no common prefix, return the empty string.

edgeCases: An empty string anywhere in the array forces an empty result.
A single string is its own prefix.
The prefix can never exceed the shortest string's length.

complexity.naive: O(n * m) but wasteful — compare all strings fully before truncating.
complexity.target: O(total characters) time — scan character positions across all strings, stopping at the first mismatch or the shortest string's end.

problems.title: Roman to Integer
problems.problem: Given a roman numeral string, convert it to an integer. Symbols: I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1000. A smaller symbol placed before a larger one means subtraction (IV = 4, IX = 9, CM = 900).

Repeated symbols simply add.

complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — sum each symbol's value, subtracting instead of adding whenever a symbol is smaller than the one after it.

problems.title: String to Integer (atoi)
problems.problem: Implement atoi: skip leading whitespace, read an optional '+' or '-' sign, then read as many digits as possible and stop at the first non-digit. Clamp the result to the 32-bit signed range [-2^31, 2^31 - 1]. Return 0 if no digits.

Out-of-range values clamp to the 32-bit bound rather than wrapping.

complexity.naive: parseInt gets most cases right but does not clamp to the 32-bit range.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — a small state machine: whitespace, then sign, then digits, clamping as you accumulate.

problems.title: Reverse Words in a String
problems.problem: Given a string `s`, reverse the order of the words. Words are separated by one or more spaces. The result must have single spaces between words and no leading or trailing space.
constraints: s contains English letters, digits and spaces, and has at least one word.

reverseWords("a good   example")  ->  "example good a"   // space runs collapse
reverseWords("hello")             ->  "hello"            // a lone word is unchanged
edgeCases: Leading and trailing spaces must be stripped.
Multiple spaces between words collapse into one.
Word ORDER reverses; the letters inside each word do not.

complexity.naive: Splitting naively on a single space produces empty strings that must be filtered.
complexity.target: O(n) time — split on runs of whitespace, reverse the list, and join with single spaces. (O(1) space in place: reverse the whole string, then each word.)

problems.title: Zigzag Conversion
problems.problem: Write the string `s` in a zigzag pattern across `numRows` rows, then read it off row by row and return the resulting string.
constraints: s consists of English letters, ',' and '.'.
edgeCases: numRows = 1 returns the input unchanged.
numRows >= s.length also returns the input unchanged.
The direction flips at the top AND bottom rows.

complexity.naive: Physically building a numRows x n character matrix wastes O(n * numRows) space.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(n) space — append each character to a per-row buffer, flipping the row direction at the first and last row, then concatenate the rows.

problems.title: Multiply Strings
problems.problem: Given two non-negative integers represented as strings, return their product, also as a string. You may not convert them to a built-in big-integer type directly.
constraints: Both consist of digits only and have no leading zeros except "0" itself.
edgeCases: Either operand being "0" makes the product "0".
Leading zeros must be stripped from the result.
The product of an m- and an n-digit number has at most m + n digits.

complexity.naive: Repeated string addition (adding num1 to itself num2 times) is astronomically slow.
complexity.target: O(m * n) time — schoolbook multiplication into an (m + n) digit array, where digit i of num1 and j of num2 land at position i + j + 1, then carry.

problems.title: Spiral Matrix
problems.problem: Given an m x n matrix, return all its elements in spiral order: right across the top, down the right side, left across the bottom, up the left side, then inward.
edgeCases: A single row or single column must not be traversed twice.
Non-square matrices.

complexity.naive: Marking visited cells in a parallel grid works but costs O(m * n) extra space.
complexity.target: O(m * n) time, O(1) extra space — four boundary pointers (top, bottom, left, right) contracted after each pass.

problems.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
problems.problem: Given an m x n matrix, if an element is 0 set its entire row and column to 0. You must do it IN PLACE.
examples: The matrix is mutated in place; the result shown is the matrix afterwards.
edgeCases: A matrix that is already all zeroes.
FOLLOW-UP
Could you devise a constant O(1) space solution?

complexity.naive: O(m * n) extra space — a full copy of the matrix, or O(m + n) with row and column
complexity.target: O(m * n) time, O(1) space — use the first row and column themselves as the marker storage, with two flags for whether they originally held a zero.

problems.title: Search a 2D Matrix
problems.problem: Given an m x n matrix where each row is sorted ascending and the first value of each row is greater than the last value of the previous row, return true if `target` is present. Must run in O(log(m * n)) time.
edgeCases: A target smaller or larger than everything.
A 1x1 matrix.

complexity.naive: O(m * n) time — scan every cell, ignoring the sorted structure.
complexity.target: O(log(m * n)) time — binary search the matrix as a flat array, mapping index i to (row = i / n, col = i % n).

problems.title: Valid Sudoku
problems.problem: Determine whether a 9 x 9 Sudoku board is valid. Only the filled cells need checking: each row, each column and each of the nine 3 x 3 sub-boxes must contain the digits 1-9 without repetition. The board need not be solvable.

examples: A standard partially filled valid board                ->  true
The same board with an extra 8 in the top-left box     ->  false
An entirely empty board ('.' everywhere)               ->  true
A board with exactly one filled cell                   ->  true
Two 1s in the same row (or the same column)            ->  false
Two 1s in one 3x3 box, in different rows and columns   ->  false
edgeCases: An empty board is valid.
Only filled cells are checked; the board need not be solvable.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) per constraint with three separate full passes over the board.
complexity.target: O(1) time (the board is fixed at 81 cells) — a single pass maintaining 9 row sets, 9 column sets and 9 box sets.

problems.title: Game of Life
problems.problem: Given an m x n board of 1 (live) and 0 (dead) cells, compute the next state under Conway's rules: a live cell with fewer than 2 or more than 3 live neighbors dies, a live cell with 2 or 3 survives, and a dead cell with exactly 3 becomes live. All cells update SIMULTANEOUSLY, and you should do it in place.

Cells on the border have fewer than 8 neighbors.
Neighbors include all 8 directions, diagonals included.
FOLLOW-UP
Could you solve it in-place? Remember that the board needs to be updated simultaneously.
The board is theoretically infinite. How would you handle the live cells at the border?

complexity.naive: O(m * n) extra space — copy the board and read neighbors from the copy.
complexity.target: O(m * n) time, O(1) space — encode both states in each cell (e.g. 2 means was-dead- now-live), then normalise in a second pass.

problems.title: Implement Queue using Stacks
problems.problem: Implement a FIFO queue using only two stacks. Support push(x), pop(), peek() and empty(). You may only use standard stack operations. Each operation should be O(1) AMORTIZED.

complexity.naive: O(n) per operation — shuttle all elements between the stacks on every push or pop.
complexity.target: O(1) amortized — an input stack for pushes and an output stack for pops, refilled only when it runs empty.

problems.title: Design HashMap
problems.problem: Design a HashMap without using any built-in hash table library. Support put(key, value), get(key) returning -1 if absent, and remove(key).

m.remove(99);                    // removing an absent key is a no-op
m.put(0, 0); m.get(0)   ->  0    // 0 is a legal key and a legal value

put on an existing key updates rather than duplicating.
Collisions must be handled — this is the point of the exercise.

complexity.naive: A single array of size 10^6 works here but does not generalize and wastes memory.
complexity.target: O(1) average — an array of buckets indexed by hash, each bucket a list handling collisions by chaining.

problems.title: Design Circular Queue
problems.problem: Design a circular queue of fixed capacity: enQueue(value), deQueue(), Front(), Rear(), isEmpty() and isFull(). The unused space in front of the queue must be reusable.
constraints: new MyCircularQueue(k)              initialize the queue with capacity k
enQueue(value)          -> boolean  insert value at the rear; return whether it succeeded
deQueue()               -> boolean  delete the element at the front; return whether it
Front()                 -> number   return the front element, or -1 if the queue is empty
Rear()                  -> number   return the rear element, or -1 if the queue is empty
isEmpty()               -> boolean  return true if the queue is empty
isFull()                -> boolean  return true if the queue is full

complexity.naive: Shifting all elements on dequeue is O(n) per operation.
complexity.target: O(1) per operation — a fixed array with head and tail indices advanced modulo capacity, plus a size field.

problems.title: Flatten Nested List Iterator
problems.problem: You are given a nested list of integers, where each element is either an integer or a list whose elements are also integers or lists. Implement an iterator with next() and hasNext() that flattens it.

new NestedIterator([[], [1], [], [2, [3]]])  ->  [1, 2, 3]   // empty lists are skipped

Nesting can be arbitrarily deep.
hasNext() may need to descend through several empty lists before answering.

problems.title: Design Twitter
problems.problem: Design a simplified Twitter: postTweet(userId, tweetId), getNewsFeed(userId) returning the 10 most recent tweet ids from the user and those they follow (most recent first), follow(followerId, followeeId) and unfollow(followerId, followeeId).
constraints: postTweet(userId, tweetId)        -> void      compose a new tweet; each tweetId is used at

follow(followerId, followeeId)    -> void      followerId starts following followeeId
unfollow(followerId, followeeId)  -> void      followerId stops following followeeId

t.unfollow(1, 3);                                // never followed — a harmless no-op

Following yourself must not duplicate tweets.
Unfollowing someone you do not follow must not throw.

complexity.naive: O(total tweets) per feed — gather every tweet from every followee and sort them all.
complexity.target: O(k log f) per feed — keep each user's tweets newest-first with a global timestamp, then merge the followees' lists with a heap, stopping after 10.

problems.title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
problems.problem: Given `n` nodes labelled 0..n-1 and a list of undirected edges, return the number of connected components in the graph.
constraints: There are no repeated edges and no self-loops.
edgeCases: No edges means every node is its own component.
Isolated nodes still count.
The graph may be disconnected in several places at once.

complexity.naive: Running a fresh search from every node without tracking visits re-walks components
complexity.target: O(E * a(N)) with union-find — start the count at n and decrement on each successful union. DFS/BFS over unvisited nodes is O(V + E) and equally valid.

problems.title: Graph Valid Tree
problems.problem: Given `n` nodes labelled 0..n-1 and a list of undirected edges, determine whether they form a valid tree: fully connected and containing no cycles.
constraints: There are no self-loops or repeated edges.
examples: validTree(1, [])                               ->  true   // single node, no edges
validTree(3, [[0,1],[1,2]])                    ->  true   // a path is a tree
validTree(4, [[0,1],[1,2],[0,2]])              ->  false  // n-1 edges, still not connected
edgeCases: A tree on n nodes has EXACTLY n - 1 edges.
Correct edge count is not sufficient; it must also be connected.
A single node with no edges is a valid tree.

complexity.naive: Checking connectivity and cycles with two independent passes duplicates work.
complexity.target: O(E * a(N)) with union-find — reject if any union joins two nodes already in the same set, then confirm exactly one set remains.

problems.title: Redundant Connection
problems.problem: A tree had one extra edge added, producing a graph with exactly one cycle. Given the edge list, return the edge that can be removed to restore a tree. If several qualify, return the one appearing LAST in the input.
constraints: edges[i] = [a, b] with 1 <= a < b <= n
The graph is connected and contains exactly one cycle.
edgeCases: Several edges may lie on the cycle — return the LAST one in input order.
Nodes are 1-indexed, not 0-indexed.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — remove each edge in turn and test whether the rest forms a tree.
complexity.target: O(n * a(n)) time — union-find in input order: the first edge whose endpoints already share a root is the answer.

problems.title: Accounts Merge
problems.problem: Each account is [name, email1, email2, ...]. Two accounts belong to the same person if they share any email; names may be shared by different people. Merge them and return each account as its name followed by its emails in sorted order.
examples: ->  [["John","a@m.com"], ["John","b@m.com"]]   // same name, no shared email — two people
->  [["Zed","a@m.com","b@m.com","c@m.com"]]   // emails come out sorted, not in input order
edgeCases: The same NAME does not imply the same person — only a shared email does.
Merging is transitive: A shares with B, B with C, so all three merge.
Output emails must be sorted; the account order need not be.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — compare every pair of accounts for a shared email and merge repeatedly
complexity.target: O(n * k * log) time — union-find keyed by email (or DFS over an email graph), then group emails by root and sort each group.

problems.title: Course Schedule II
problems.problem: Given `numCourses` and a list of prerequisite pairs [a, b] meaning b must be taken before a, return any valid ordering in which all courses can be finished. If it is impossible, return an empty array.
examples: findOrder(3, [])                         ->  [0, 1, 2]   // no prerequisites — any order accepted
findOrder(3, [[0,1],[1,2]])              ->  [2, 1, 0]   // a chain forces one order
edgeCases: A cycle means no ordering exists — return an empty array.
Courses with no prerequisites can appear anywhere valid.
Several orderings may be correct; any one is accepted.

complexity.naive: Trying permutations and validating each is factorial in numCourses.
complexity.target: O(V + E) time — topological sort: Kahn's algorithm on in-degrees, or DFS post-order reversed. A result shorter than numCourses proves a cycle.

problems.title: Network Delay Time
problems.problem: You are given `times` as directed edges [u, v, w] meaning a signal takes w time to go from u to v, a node count `n` and a start node `k`. Return the time for all nodes to receive the signal, or -1 if some never do.
examples: networkDelayTime([[1,2,1],[2,3,2],[1,3,4]], 3, 1)  ->  3   // via node 2 (3) beats the direct edge (4)
edgeCases: An unreachable node makes the answer -1.
The answer is the MAXIMUM of all shortest paths, not their sum.
Edges are directed — [u,v,w] does not imply [v,u,w].

complexity.naive: A plain BFS ignores edge weights and gives the wrong answer on weighted graphs.
complexity.target: O(E log V) time — Dijkstra from k with a min-heap, then return the largest finalised distance (or -1 if any node was never reached).

problems.title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
problems.problem: Given points on a 2D plane, the cost of connecting two points is their Manhattan distance. Return the minimum total cost to connect all points so that there is exactly one path between any two.
edgeCases: A single point costs 0.
Manhattan distance is |x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|, not Euclidean.
The graph is complete — every pair is a candidate edge.

complexity.naive: Enumerating spanning trees is astronomically expensive.
complexity.target: Minimum spanning tree — Prim's with a heap is O(n^2 log n) here (the graph is dense), or Kruskal's with union-find over all O(n^2) edges.

problems.title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
problems.problem: Given `n` cities, a list of flights [from, to, price], a source, a destination and an integer `k`, return the cheapest price from src to dst using AT MOST k stops, or -1 if no such route exists.
edgeCases: k counts STOPS, so k + 1 flights are allowed.
The cheapest overall route may exceed the stop limit and be invalid.
An unreachable destination returns -1.

complexity.naive: Plain Dijkstra can discard a costlier path that uses fewer stops and would have been
complexity.target: O(k * E) time — Bellman-Ford relaxed exactly k + 1 times over a snapshot of the previous round's costs (or BFS by levels).

problems.title: Reconstruct Itinerary
problems.problem: Given a list of airline tickets [from, to], reconstruct the itinerary in order. All tickets belong to a man departing from "JFK" and must be used exactly once. If several valid itineraries exist, return the smallest in lexical order.
constraints: At least one valid itinerary is guaranteed.
examples: ->  ["JFK","ATL"]   // one ticket, the smallest possible input
->  ["JFK","ATL","JFK","SFO"]   // ATL is taken first, being lexically smaller
->  ["JFK","NRT","JFK","KUL"]   // taking KUL first would strand the trip
->  ["JFK","ATL","JFK","ATL"]   // duplicate tickets, each used exactly once
edgeCases: EVERY ticket must be used exactly once.
Duplicate tickets between the same pair are allowed.

complexity.naive: Backtracking over every permutation of tickets is factorial.
complexity.target: O(E log E) time — Hierholzer's algorithm for an Eulerian path: visit destinations in sorted order, and append an airport to the result only once it has no unused tickets left, then reverse.

problems.title: Merge Sorted Array
problems.problem: You are given two sorted arrays `nums1` (with m real values followed by n zeroes as spare room) and `nums2` (with n values). Merge nums2 into nums1 IN PLACE so nums1 ends up sorted.

merge([-1,3,0,0], 2, [-2,0], 2)      ->  [-2,-1,0,3]   // negatives, and a real 0 in nums2
edgeCases: m = 0 means nums1 holds only spare room.
n = 0 leaves nums1 unchanged.
FOLLOW-UP
Can you come up with an algorithm that runs in O(m + n) time?

complexity.naive: O((m + n) log(m + n)) time — concatenate then sort, throwing away the sorted
complexity.target: O(m + n) time, O(1) space — fill from the BACK, comparing the tails of both arrays, so no unread value is ever overwritten.

problems.title: Sort an Array
problems.problem: Given an array `nums`, sort it in ascending order WITHOUT using any built-in sort. The solution must run in O(n log n) time and use the smallest space possible.
edgeCases: Duplicates must be preserved, not collapsed.
Already-sorted or reverse-sorted input.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — bubble, selection or insertion sort. Fine to write once for
complexity.target: O(n log n) time — merge sort (O(n) space, stable, predictable) or heapsort (O(1) space). This is the problem for actually IMPLEMENTING a sort.

problems.title: Insertion Sort List
problems.problem: Given the head of a singly linked list, sort it using INSERTION SORT and return the sorted head. Insertion sort repeatedly removes the next element and inserts it into its correct position in the sorted prefix.
constraints: `head` is a ListNode object, not an array. The arrays in EXAMPLES list the node values in
order; the test runner links them into real nodes before calling your function.
edgeCases: A single node is already sorted.
An already-sorted list is the best case, O(n).

problems.title: Largest Number
problems.problem: Given a list of non-negative integers `nums`, arrange them so they form the largest possible number, and return it as a string.
examples: largestNumber([432, 43243])       ->  "43243432"   // the longer number does not win by length
edgeCases: All zeros must produce "0", not a string of zeroes.
The result may exceed the safe integer range — keep it a string.

complexity.naive: Trying every permutation is O(n!) and infeasible past a handful of numbers.

problems.title: Find Pivot Index
problems.problem: Given an array `nums`, return the leftmost index where the sum of everything strictly to its left equals the sum of everything strictly to its right. Return -1 if no such index exists.

pivotIndex([1])                 ->  0   // single element, both sides empty
pivotIndex([-1, 1, 0])          ->  2   // the last index qualifies the same way
pivotIndex([0, 0, 0])           ->  0   // every index qualifies — return the leftmost
edgeCases: Index 0 is valid — the empty left side sums to 0.
The last index is valid the same way.
Return the LEFTMOST qualifying index.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — recompute both side sums at every index.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(1) space — one pass with a running left sum, comparing it against (total - left - nums[i]).

problems.title: Range Sum Query - Immutable
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums`, handle many queries asking for the sum of the elements between indices left and right inclusive. Implement the NumArray class with sumRange(left, right).
