sumRange(left, right)  -> number  return the sum of nums[left..right] inclusive

complexity.naive: O(n) per query — sum the range each time. With 10^4 queries on 10^4 elements this is
complexity.target: O(n) preprocessing, O(1) per query — a prefix-sum array where sumRange(l, r) = prefix[r + 1] - prefix[l].

problems.title: Range Sum Query 2D - Immutable
problems.problem: Given a 2D matrix, handle queries for the sum of the rectangle defined by its upper left and lower right corners. Implement NumMatrix with sumRegion(row1, col1, row2, col2).
constraints: new NumMatrix(matrix)                         initialize the object with the integer matrix
sumRegion(row1, col1, row2, col2)  -> number  return the sum of the rectangle with those
edgeCases: A single-cell rectangle where row1 = row2 and col1 = col2.

complexity.naive: O(m * n) per query — sum the rectangle cell by cell.
complexity.target: O(m * n) preprocessing, O(1) per query — a 2D prefix sum, then sum = BR - TR - BL + TL by inclusion-exclusion.

problems.title: Continuous Subarray Sum
problems.problem: Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return true if there is a contiguous subarray of length AT LEAST TWO whose sum is a multiple of k.
examples: checkSubarraySum([0, 0], 1)             ->  true   // 0 is a multiple of every k
checkSubarraySum([5], 5)                ->  false  // one element, length must be >= 2
edgeCases: The subarray must have length >= 2 — a single multiple of k does not count.
0 is a multiple of every k, so [0, 0] returns true.

complexity.naive: O(n^2) time — sum every subarray and test divisibility.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(k) space — a map of prefix-sum REMAINDER to its earliest index; a repeated remainder at least two indices apart proves a valid subarray.

problems.title: Happy Number
problems.problem: A happy number is defined by repeatedly replacing the number with the sum of the squares of its digits; it is happy if this reaches 1. Given `n`, return true if it is happy.
edgeCases: Unhappy numbers always fall into a CYCLE — you must detect it or loop forever.
1 is happy by definition.

complexity.naive: Looping without cycle detection never terminates for an unhappy number.
complexity.target: O(log n) time, O(1) space — Floyd's cycle detection with a slow and a fast digit- square-sum pointer. A visited Set is simpler but O(log n) space.

problems.title: Sqrt(x)
problems.problem: Given a non-negative integer `x`, return the square root of x rounded DOWN to the nearest integer. You may not use any built-in exponent or square root function.
examples: mySqrt(2147395600)  ->  46340   // a perfect square near the upper bound
edgeCases: x = 0 and x = 1 return themselves.
The result is TRUNCATED, never rounded up.

complexity.naive: O(sqrt(x)) time — increment a counter until its square exceeds x.
complexity.target: O(log x) time — binary search over [0, x] for the largest integer whose square does not exceed x. (Newton's method converges even faster.)

problems.title: Count Primes
problems.problem: Given an integer `n`, return the number of prime numbers strictly less than n.
edgeCases: n = 0, 1 and 2 all return 0.
The bound is STRICT — n itself is never counted.

complexity.naive: O(n * sqrt(n)) time — test each number for primality by trial division. Too slow at n
complexity.target: O(n log log n) time, O(n) space — the Sieve of Eratosthenes, marking multiples of each prime starting from its square.

problems.title: Ugly Number II
problems.problem: An ugly number has no prime factors other than 2, 3 and 5. Given an integer `n`, return the nth ugly number (1-indexed). By convention 1 is ugly.
examples: nthUglyNumber(1)     ->  1   // 1 is the first ugly number
nthUglyNumber(11)    ->  15  // 14 is skipped — it has the factor 7
edgeCases: 1 counts as the first ugly number.
Duplicates must be skipped: 6 arises as both 2*3 and 3*2.

complexity.naive: O(n * k) time — check each integer in turn by dividing out 2s, 3s and 5s.
complexity.target: O(n) time, O(n) space — three pointers into the growing sequence, taking the minimum of (2*a, 3*b, 5*c) each step and advancing EVERY pointer that produced it.
